newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Ex-rebel leader says MRTA made fatal mistakes. [CORRECTED 20:23 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Ex-rebel leader says MRTA made fatal mistakes. [CORRECTED 20:23 GMT]

text.p: An ex-rebel leader who held 17 diplomats hostage at the Dominican embassy in Bogota for 61 days in 1980 said on Wednesday that the takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima was fatally flawed from the start.

(Corrects to add dropped word "residence") Among other mistakes, according to Rosemberg Pabon, a leader of the now defunct M-19 guerrilla group, Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels lacked a forceful leader outside the embassy residence to press for a negotiated settlement.
"We had the good fortune of having our maximum leader, Jaime Bateman, on the outside," Pabon told Reuters, recalling the tense standoff that led a negotiated settlement 17 years ago this month.
A U.S. ambassador was among the hostages held by a small group of M-19 commandos led by Pabon, who was known at the time as "Comandante Uno."

"He (Bateman) was able to assess the situation with more flexibility than us -- those of us who were in the embassy and the political prisoners themselves," Pabon said in a telephone interview. "He looked for and found a political way out. In Peru, their maximum leader, Victor Polai, was in jail and held totally incommunicado," he added.

"Other people who might have been able to help them like Isaac Velazco didn't have enough strength," Pabon said, referring to the MRTA's European-based spokesman. Pointing a finger of blame at Velazco, he added that he was "very dogmatic and intransigent" in the crisis that ended Tuesday with the death of his 14 comrades.

Apart from the lack of a forceful negotiator outside the besieged embassy residence, Pabon said the Peruvian rebels led by Nestor Cerpa committed the mistake of falling into a daily routine. "Routine is something that works against you in these situations," Pabon said.
He noted that that Cerpa and other rebels were reportedly unarmed and playing a daily soccer game when security forces launched their stunning assault on the embassy residence.
"We were careful and took measures to avoid an assault. We avoided routine and we changed the position of the hostages regularly," Pabon said.

The M-19, one of Latin America's most flamboyant guerrilla groups, was active from 1974 until 1990, when most of its members accepted government peace terms and laid down their arms to form a political party.

The group is best known for its takeover of Bogota's Palace of Justice by 35 M-19 commandos in November 1985. Colombia's military responded by launching a 27-hour siege of the courts building in which more than 100 people -- including 11 Supreme Court justices -- were killed.
